chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The men quickly found their horses in the half-darkness, tightened saddle girths, and formed into companies. Denisov stood by the watchman's hut, giving final orders. The detachment's infantry filed along the road and quickly vanished among the trees in the mist of early dawn, hundreds of feet splashing through the mud. The esaul gave orders to his men. Petya held his horse by the bridle, impatiently awaiting the command to mount. His face, freshly washed in cold water, was glowing, and his eyes were especially bright. Cold shivers ran down his spine and his whole body pulsed rhythmically.
"Well, is everything ready?" asked Denisov. "Bring the horses."

The horses were brought. Denisov scolded the Cossack because the saddle girths were too loose, then mounted. Petya put his foot in the stirrup. His horse, out of habit, made as if to nip his leg, but Petya leaped quickly into the saddle, unaware of his own weight, and turning to look at the hussars moving up in the darkness behind him, rode up to Denisov.
"Vasili Dmitrich, give me something to do! Please... for God's sake!" he said.
Denisov seemed to have forgotten Petya even existed. He turned to glance at him.
"I ask one thing of you," he said sternly, "obey me and don't push yourself into anything."

He didn't say another word to Petya the entire ride. When they reached the forest's edge, it was noticeably getting lighter over the field. Denisov whispered with the esaul, and the Cossacks began riding past Petya and Denisov. When they had all gone by, Denisov spurred his horse and rode down the hill. Slipping and sliding on their haunches, the horses carried their riders down into the ravine. Petya rode beside Denisov, the pulse of excitement in his body growing constantly stronger. It was getting lighter and lighter, but the mist still hid distant objects. Reaching the valley, Denisov looked back and nodded to a Cossack beside him.
"The signal!" he said.
The Cossack raised his arm, and a shot rang out. Instantly the sound of galloping hooves was heard, shouts broke out from all sides, and more shots followed.

At the first sound of pounding hooves and shouting, Petya whipped his horse and let the reins go slack, galloping forward without heeding Denisov, who yelled after him. It seemed to Petya that at the instant the shot was fired, it suddenly became as bright as noon. He galloped toward the bridge. Cossacks were racing along the road ahead of him. On the bridge he crashed into a Cossack who had fallen behind, but galloped on. In front of him, soldiers—probably French—were running from right to left across the road. One of them fell in the mud under his horse's hooves.

Cossacks were crowding around a hut, doing something. From the middle of the crowd came terrible screams. Petya galloped up, and the first thing he saw was the pale face and trembling jaw of a Frenchman clutching the shaft of a lance aimed at him.
"Hurrah!... Boys!... Ours!" shouted Petya, and giving his excited horse free rein, he galloped forward along the village street.

He could hear gunfire ahead. Cossacks, hussars, and ragged Russian prisoners who had come running from both sides of the road were shouting something loudly and incoherently. A dashing-looking Frenchman in a blue overcoat, bareheaded and with a frowning red face, had been fighting off the hussars. By the time Petya galloped up, the Frenchman had already fallen. "Too late again!" flashed through Petya's mind, and he galloped on toward the place where the rapid gunfire was coming from. The shots came from the yard of the landowner's house he had visited the night before with Dolokhov. The French were making a stand behind a wattle fence in a garden thick with bushes, firing at the Cossacks crowding at the gate. Through the smoke, as he approached, Petya saw Dolokhov, his face a pale greenish tint, shouting to his men. "Go around! Wait for the infantry!" he yelled as Petya rode up.
"Wait?... Hurrah!" shouted Petya, and without pausing for an instant, he galloped toward the place where the gunfire was thickest and the smoke was densest.

A volley rang out. Some bullets whistled past; others smacked into something. The Cossacks and Dolokhov galloped after Petya through the gateway into the courtyard. In the dense, wavering smoke, some of the French threw down their weapons and ran out of the bushes to meet the Cossacks, while others fled down the hill toward the pond. Petya was galloping across the courtyard, but instead of holding the reins, he was waving both arms about rapidly and strangely, slipping further and further to one side of his saddle. His horse, having galloped up to a campfire smoldering in the morning light, stopped suddenly, and Petya fell heavily onto the wet ground. The Cossacks saw his arms and legs jerk rapidly, though his head was completely still. A bullet had pierced his skull.

After speaking to the senior French officer—who came out of the house with a white handkerchief tied to his sword, announcing their surrender—Dolokhov dismounted and went over to Petya, who lay motionless with his arms flung out.
"Done for!" he said with a frown, and walked to the gate to meet Denisov, who was riding toward him.
"Killed?" cried Denisov, recognizing from a distance the unmistakable, horribly familiar posture of Petya's lifeless body.

"Done for!" Dolokhov repeated, as if saying the words gave him a kind of grim satisfaction, and he walked quickly to the prisoners, who were surrounded by Cossacks. "We won't be taking them!" he called out to Denisov.
Denisov didn't reply. He rode up to Petya, dismounted, and with trembling hands turned toward himself the bloodstained, mud-covered face that had already gone white.

"I like having something sweet. Raisins—wonderful ones... take them all!" The words came back to him. And the Cossacks looked around in surprise at the sound—like the yelp of a dog—with which Denisov turned away, walked to the wattle fence, and gripped it.
Among the Russian prisoners rescued by Denisov and Dolokhov was Pierre Bezukhov.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Throughout the entire march from Moscow, no new orders had been given by the French authorities regarding the group of prisoners that included Pierre. By October twenty-second, their party was no longer traveling with the same troops and supply wagons they had left Moscow with. Half the hardtack wagons that had accompanied them on the first legs of the journey had been captured by Cossacks; the other half had gone on ahead. Not one of the dismounted cavalrymen who had marched at the front of the prisoner column remained—they had all disappeared. The artillery the prisoners had seen ahead of them during the early days had been replaced by Marshal Junot's enormous baggage train, escorted by Westphalians. Behind the prisoners came a cavalry baggage train.

From Vyazma onward, the French army, which had until then been moving in three columns, continued as a single mass. The symptoms of disorder that Pierre had first noticed at their initial stopping place after leaving Moscow had now reached their ultimate extreme.

The road they traveled was bordered on both sides by dead horses. Ragged men who had fallen behind from various regiments constantly drifted in and out, sometimes joining the moving column, sometimes dropping behind again.

Several times during the march, false alarms had been raised. The escort soldiers would grab their muskets, fire, and run in a panic, trampling one another, only to reassemble afterward and curse each other for the needless fright.
These three groups traveling together—the cavalry stores, the convoy of prisoners, and Junot's baggage train—still formed a separate and unified whole, though each group was rapidly shrinking.

Of the artillery baggage train, which had originally consisted of a hundred and twenty wagons, no more than sixty remained; the rest had been captured or abandoned. Several of Junot's wagons had also been seized or left behind. Three wagons had been raided and looted by stragglers from Davout's corps. From the talk of the Germans, Pierre learned that a larger guard had been assigned to that baggage train than to the prisoners, and that one of their comrades, a German soldier, had been shot on the marshal's direct order because a silver spoon belonging to the marshal had been found in his possession.

The group of prisoners had shrunk the most. Of the three hundred and thirty men who had set out from Moscow, fewer than a hundred now remained. The prisoners were more burdensome to their escort than even the cavalry saddles or Junot's baggage. They all understood that the saddles and Junot's spoon might have some use, but that cold and hungry soldiers should have to stand guard over equally cold and hungry Russians who kept freezing and collapsing on the road—at which point the order was to shoot them—was not merely incomprehensible but revolting. And the escort, as if afraid that giving in to the pity they felt for the prisoners would only make their own situation worse, treated them with particular harshness and cruelty.

At Dorogobuzh, while the convoy soldiers had locked the prisoners in a stable and gone off to loot their own supply stores, several prisoner soldiers tunneled under the wall and escaped, but they were recaptured by the French and shot.

The earlier arrangement of keeping officer prisoners separate from the rest had long since been abandoned. All who could walk went together, and after the third stage Pierre had rejoined Karataev and the gray-blue, bandy-legged dog that had adopted Karataev as its master.

On the third day after leaving Moscow, Karataev fell ill again with the fever he had suffered from in the Moscow hospital, and as he grew gradually weaker, Pierre began keeping his distance. He did not know why, but ever since Karataev had begun to deteriorate, it cost Pierre an effort to go near him. When he did approach and heard the quiet moaning with which Karataev usually lay down at each stopping place, and when he smelled the odor coming from him—now stronger than before—Pierre would move farther away and try not to think about him.

While imprisoned in the shed, Pierre had learned—not through his intellect but with his whole being, through life itself—that human beings are made for happiness, that happiness lies within us in the satisfaction of simple human needs, and that all unhappiness comes not from deprivation but from excess. And now, during these last three weeks of marching, he had learned yet another new and comforting truth: that nothing in this world is truly terrible. He had learned that just as there is no condition in which a person can be completely happy and entirely free, there is no condition in which one must be completely unhappy and lack all freedom. He learned that suffering and freedom have their limits, and that those limits are very close together; that the person lying in a bed of roses with one crumpled petal suffered as keenly as he now did, sleeping on bare damp earth with one side growing cold while the other warmed; and that when he had once worn tight dancing shoes, he had suffered just as much as he did now walking with bare feet covered in sores—his footwear having long since fallen apart. He discovered that when he had married his wife—seemingly of his own free will—he had been no more free than now, when they locked him in a stable at night. Of all the things he later called his sufferings, but which at the time he barely felt, the worst was the state of his bare, raw, scab-covered feet. (The horsemeat was actually appetizing and nourishing; the saltpeter flavor of the gunpowder they used instead of salt was even pleasant; there was no great cold; it was always warm walking during the day; and at night there were campfires; the lice that devoured him actually warmed his body.) The one thing that was initially hard to bear was his feet.

After the second day's march, Pierre examined his feet by the campfire and thought it would be impossible to walk on them. But when everyone got up, he went along limping, and once he had warmed up, walked without feeling the pain, though at night his feet looked more terrible than before. But he no longer looked at them and thought of other things instead.

Only now did Pierre truly grasp the full strength of life in a person and the saving power of being able to shift one's attention from one thing to another—like the safety valve on a boiler that releases excess steam when the pressure becomes too great.

He did not see and did not hear them shooting the prisoners who fell behind, though more than a hundred died that way. He did not think of Karataev, who grew weaker every day and would clearly soon share the same fate. Still less did Pierre think about himself. The harder his situation became and the more terrible the future, the more independent of his circumstances were the joyful and comforting thoughts, memories, and imaginings that came to him.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: At midday on October twenty-second, Pierre was trudging uphill along the muddy, slippery road, looking at his feet and at the roughness of the way. Occasionally he glanced at the familiar crowd around him, then back at his feet again. Both were equally familiar and felt like part of himself. The blue-gray, bandy-legged dog ran merrily alongside the road, sometimes lifting one hind leg to hop along on three as proof of its agility and good spirits, then going on all four again and rushing off to bark at crows sitting on carrion. The dog was merrier and sleeker than it had been in Moscow. All around lay the flesh of different creatures—from humans to horses—in various stages of decay; and since wolves were kept away by the passing men, the dog could eat all it wanted.

It had been raining since morning, seeming as though it might stop any minute and the sky clear, but after a brief pause it rained harder than before. The saturated road no longer absorbed the water, which ran along the ruts in streams.
Pierre walked along looking from side to side, counting his steps in threes and ticking them off on his fingers. Mentally addressing the rain, he repeated: "Come on now, come on! Pour harder!"

He seemed to be thinking of nothing, but deep down inside him, his soul was occupied with something important and comforting. This something was a very subtle spiritual insight drawn from a conversation with Karataev the day before.

At their previous stopping place, feeling chilled by a dying campfire, Pierre had gotten up and gone to the next one, which was burning better. There Platon Karataev sat covered up—head and all—with his greatcoat as if it were a vestment, telling the soldiers in his warm and pleasant, though now weakened voice, a story Pierre already knew. It was past midnight, the hour when Karataev was usually free of his fever and especially lively. When Pierre reached the fire and heard Platon's voice, weakened by illness, and saw his thin face brightly lit by the blaze, he felt a painful stab in his heart. His feeling of pity for this man frightened him, and he wanted to leave, but there was no other fire, so Pierre sat down, trying not to look at Platon.
"Well, how are you?" he asked.
"How am I? If we complain about sickness, God won't grant us death," replied Platon, and immediately resumed the story he had begun.
"And so, brother," he continued, with a smile on his pale, wasted face and a particularly joyful light in his eyes, "you see, brother..."

Pierre had long been familiar with that story. Karataev had told it to him alone some half-dozen times, always with a special joyful emotion. But though he knew it well, Pierre now listened as though it were something new, and the quiet rapture Karataev clearly felt as he told it communicated itself to Pierre as well. The story was about an old merchant who lived a good and God-fearing life with his family, and who once went to the Nizhni fair with a companion—a rich merchant.

Having checked into an inn, they both went to sleep, and the next morning the companion was found robbed and with his throat cut. A blood-stained knife was found under the old merchant's pillow. He was tried, flogged, and his nostrils torn off, "all in proper form" as Karataev put it, and he was sent to hard labor in Siberia.

"And so, brother" (it was at this point that Pierre had come up), "ten years or more passed. The old man was living as a convict, accepting his lot as he should and doing no wrong. He only prayed to God for death. Well, one night the convicts were gathered together just as we are, with the old man among them. And they began telling what each was being punished for and how they had sinned against God. One told how he had taken a life, another had taken two, a third had set a house on fire, while another had simply been a vagrant and done nothing wrong. So they asked the old man: 'What are you being punished for, old father?' 'I, my dear brothers,' said he, 'am being punished for my own and other men's sins. But I have not killed anyone or taken anything that was not mine—I have only helped my poorer brothers. I was a merchant, dear brothers, and had much property.' And he went on to tell them everything in proper order. 'I don't grieve for myself,' he says, 'God, it seems, has chosen to punish me. Only I am sorry for my old wife and the children,' and the old man began to weep. Now it happened that in the group was the very man who had killed the other merchant. 'Where did it happen, old father?' he said. 'When, and in what month?' He asked about everything, and his heart began to ache. So he came up to the old man like this, and fell down at his feet! 'You are suffering because of me, old father,' he says. 'It's the absolute truth, lads, that this man,' he says, 'is being tortured innocently and for nothing! I,' he says, 'did that deed, and I slipped the knife under your head while you were asleep. Forgive me, old father,' he says, 'for Christ's sake!'"
Karataev paused, smiling joyfully as he gazed into the fire, and pushed the logs together.

"And the old man said, 'God will forgive you—we are all sinners in His sight. I suffer for my own sins,' and he wept bitter tears. Well, and what do you think, dear friends?" Karataev continued, his face brightening more and more with a radiant smile, as if what he was about to say contained the chief beauty and the whole meaning of his story: "What do you think, dear fellows? That murderer confessed to the authorities. 'I have taken six lives,' he says (he was a great sinner), 'but what I am most sorry for is this old man. Don't let him suffer because of me.' So he confessed, and it was all written down, and the papers were sent off in proper form. The place was far away, and while they were processing things, what with one thing and another, filling in all the papers in proper form—the authorities, I mean—time passed. The case reached the Tsar. Eventually the Tsar's decree came: to set the merchant free and give him the compensation that had been awarded. The paper arrived and they began looking for the old man. 'Where is the old man who has been suffering innocently and in vain? A paper has come from the Tsar!' So they began looking for him," here Karataev's lower jaw trembled, "but God had already forgiven him—he was dead! That's how it was, dear fellows!" Karataev concluded, and sat for a long time in silence, gazing before him with a smile.

And Pierre's soul was dimly but joyfully filled—not by the story itself, but by its mysterious meaning: by the radiant joy that lit up Karataev's face as he told it, and by the profound significance of that joy.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: "To your places!" a voice suddenly cried.
("To your places!")

A pleasant feeling of excitement and an expectation of something important and grand arose among both the convoy soldiers and the prisoners. From all sides came shouts of command, and from the left came smartly dressed cavalrymen on good horses, passing the prisoners at a trot. Every face showed the tension people feel at the approach of someone in authority. The prisoners crowded together and were pushed off the road. The convoy formed up.

"The Emperor! The Emperor! The Marshal! The Duke!" And hardly had the sleek cavalry passed before a carriage drawn by six gray horses rattled by. Pierre caught a glimpse of a man in a three-cornered hat with a calm expression on his handsome, plump, white face. It was one of the marshals. His eye fell on Pierre's large and striking figure, and in the expression with which he frowned and looked away, Pierre thought he detected sympathy and a desire to hide it.

The general in charge of the stores galloped after the carriage, red-faced and frightened, whipping up his thin horse. Several officers formed a group and some soldiers crowded around them. Their faces all looked excited and worried.
"What did he say? What did he say?" Pierre heard them asking.

While the marshal was passing, the prisoners had huddled together in a crowd, and Pierre saw Karataev, whom he hadn't yet seen that morning. He sat in his short overcoat, leaning against a birch tree. On his face, besides the look of joyful emotion it had worn the night before while he told the story of the merchant who suffered innocently, there was now an expression of quiet solemnity.

Karataev looked at Pierre with his kind, round eyes, now filled with tears, clearly wanting him to come closer so he could say something. But Pierre wasn't sure enough of himself. He acted as if he hadn't noticed that look and moved quickly away.

When the prisoners started walking again, Pierre looked back. Karataev was still sitting at the side of the road under the birch tree, and two Frenchmen were talking over his head. Pierre didn't look back again, but went limping up the hill.

From behind, where Karataev had been sitting, came the sound of a shot. Pierre heard it clearly, but at that moment he remembered he hadn't yet finished calculating how many stages remained to Smolensk—a calculation he had begun before the marshal went by. And he started counting again. Two French soldiers ran past Pierre, one of them carrying a lowered and still-smoking gun. They both looked pale, and in the expression on their faces—one of them glanced nervously at Pierre—there was something resembling what he had seen on the face of the young soldier at the execution. Pierre looked at the soldier and remembered that two days earlier, that man had burned his shirt while drying it at the fire and everyone had laughed at him.
Behind him, where Karataev had been sitting, the dog began to howl. "What a stupid animal! Why is it howling?" thought Pierre.

His comrades, the prisoner soldiers walking beside him, avoided looking back at the place where the shot had been fired and the dog was howling, just as Pierre did. But there was a fixed look on all their faces.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: The stores, the prisoners, and the marshal's baggage train halted at the village of Shamshevo. The men crowded together around the campfires. Pierre went up to a fire, ate some roast horsemeat, lay down with his back to the flames, and immediately fell asleep. He slept again as he had at Mozhaysk after the battle of Borodino.
Once more real events mingled with dreams, and once more someone—he or another—gave voice to his thoughts, the same thoughts that had been expressed in his dream at Mozhaysk.

"Life is everything. Life is God. Everything changes and moves, and that movement is God. And while there is life there is joy in the awareness of the divine. To love life is to love God. The hardest and most blessed thing of all is to love this life in one's sufferings, in innocent suffering."
"Karataev!" The name came into Pierre's mind.

And suddenly he saw vividly before him a long-forgotten, kindly old man who had given him geography lessons in Switzerland. "Wait a moment," said the old man, and showed Pierre a globe. This globe was alive—a vibrating sphere without fixed dimensions. Its entire surface consisted of drops pressed tightly together, and all these drops moved and shifted places, sometimes several of them merging into one, sometimes one dividing into many. Each drop tried to spread out and take up as much space as possible, but others striving to do the same compressed it, sometimes destroyed it, and sometimes merged with it.
"That is life," said the old teacher.
"How simple and clear it is," thought Pierre. "How is it I didn't know this before?"

"God is at the center, and each drop tries to expand so as to reflect Him to the greatest extent. And it grows, merges, disappears from the surface, sinks to the depths, and emerges again. There now, Karataev has spread out and disappeared. Do you understand, my child?" said the teacher.
"Do you understand, damn you?" shouted a voice, and Pierre woke up.

He lifted himself and sat up. A Frenchman who had just shoved a Russian soldier aside was squatting by the fire, roasting a piece of meat on a ramrod. His sleeves were rolled up and his sinewy, hairy, red hands with their short fingers deftly turned the ramrod. His dark, sullen face with its frowning brows was clearly visible by the glow of the coals.
"It's all the same to him," he muttered, quickly turning to a soldier standing behind him. "Scoundrel! Get away!"

And twisting the ramrod, he looked gloomily at Pierre, who turned away and gazed into the darkness. A prisoner, the Russian soldier the Frenchman had pushed away, was sitting near the fire patting something with his hand. Looking more closely, Pierre recognized the blue-gray dog sitting beside the soldier, wagging its tail.
"Ah, he's come?" said Pierre. "And Plat—" he began, but did not finish.

Suddenly and all at once a flood of memories surged through his mind—of the look Platon had given him sitting under the tree, of the shot heard from that spot, of the dog's howl, of the guilty faces of the two Frenchmen as they ran past him, of the lowered and smoking gun, and of Karataev's absence at this halt—and he was on the verge of realizing that Karataev had been killed. But at that very instant, he knew not why, a memory came to him of a summer evening he had spent with a beautiful Polish lady on the veranda of his house in Kiev. And without connecting the events of the day or drawing any conclusions from them, Pierre closed his eyes, seeing a vision of the countryside in summer mingled with memories of swimming and of the liquid, vibrating globe, and he sank into water so that it closed over his head.
Before sunrise he was awakened by shouts and rapid, heavy gunfire. French soldiers were running past him.
"The Cossacks!" one of them shouted, and a moment later a crowd of Russians surrounded Pierre.
For a long time he could not understand what was happening. All around him he heard his comrades sobbing with joy.
"Brothers! Dear fellows! Darlings!" old soldiers cried, weeping as they embraced Cossacks and hussars.

The hussars and Cossacks crowded around the prisoners. One offered them clothes, another boots, a third bread. Pierre sat among them sobbing and could not speak a word. He hugged the first soldier who came near him and kissed him, weeping.

Dolokhov stood at the gate of the ruined house, watching a stream of disarmed Frenchmen pass by. The French, agitated by everything that had happened, were talking loudly among themselves, but as they passed Dolokhov—who gently tapped his boots with his whip and watched them with cold, glassy eyes that promised nothing good—they fell silent. On the opposite side, Dolokhov's Cossack was counting the prisoners and marking each hundred with a chalk line on the gate.
"How many?" Dolokhov asked the Cossack.
"The second hundred," the Cossack replied.
"Move along, move along!" Dolokhov kept saying, having picked up this expression from the French, and when his eyes met those of the prisoners, they flashed with a cruel light.
("Move along, move along!")
Denisov, bareheaded and with a grim face, walked behind some Cossacks who were carrying the body of Petya Rostov to a grave that had been dug in the garden.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: After October twenty-eighth, when the frosts set in, the French flight took on an even more tragic character. Men froze to death or burned themselves alive at campfires, while carriages carrying people dressed in furs continued to roll past, hauling away the property that had been stolen by the Emperor, kings, and dukes. But the essential nature of the flight and disintegration of the French army continued as before.

From Moscow to Vyazma, the French army of seventy-three thousand men—not counting the Guards, who did nothing during the entire war but loot—was reduced to thirty-six thousand, though no more than five thousand had fallen in battle. From this starting point, the terms of the progression could be calculated mathematically. The French army melted away and perished at the same rate from Moscow to Vyazma, from Vyazma to Smolensk, from Smolensk to the Berezina, and from the Berezina to Vilna—regardless of the cold's intensity, the pursuit, the blocking of their path, or any other particular conditions. Beyond Vyazma, the French army stopped moving in three columns and huddled together into one mass, continuing that way to the end. Berthier wrote to his Emperor (and we know how far commanding officers allow themselves to stray from the truth when describing their army's condition), and this is what he said:

I consider it my duty to report to Your Majesty on the condition of the various corps I have had the opportunity to observe during different stages of the last two or three days' march. They are nearly disbanded. Scarcely a quarter of the soldiers remain with the standards of their regiments; the others wander off in every direction hoping to find food and escape discipline. In general, they all look to Smolensk as the place where they hope to recover. During the last few days many soldiers have been seen throwing away their cartridges and their weapons. In such circumstances, whatever your ultimate plans may be, Your Majesty's interests require that the army be reassembled at Smolensk and, first of all, freed from noncombatants—dismounted cavalry, unnecessary baggage, and artillery equipment no longer proportionate to our present forces. The soldiers, worn out by hunger and fatigue, need these supplies as well as a few days' rest. Many have died recently on the road or at camp. This state of affairs is growing worse every day and raises the fear that, unless prompt measures are taken, the troops will be beyond control in the event of a battle.
November 9: twenty miles from Smolensk.

After staggering into Smolensk—which had seemed to them a promised land—the French searched for food, killed one another, looted their own stores, and when everything had been plundered, fled farther.

They all went without knowing where or why they were going. Still less did that supposed genius, Napoleon, know it, for no one was issuing any orders to him. But he and those around him still clung to their old habits: writing commands, letters, reports, and orders of the day; calling one another "Sire," "Mon Cousin," "Prince of Eckmuhl," "King of Naples," and so on. But these orders and reports existed only on paper. Nothing in them was carried out, because nothing could be carried out. And though they addressed one another as Majesties, Highnesses, and Cousins, they all knew they were miserable wretches who had done great evil for which they now had to pay. And though they pretended to be concerned about the army, each was thinking only of himself and how to get away as quickly as possible.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: The movements of the Russian and French armies during the retreat from Moscow to the Niemen were like a game of Russian blindman's buff, where two blindfolded players stumble about and one occasionally rings a little bell to let the catcher know where he is. At first, the one with the bell rings it fearlessly, but when he gets cornered, he runs away as quietly as he can—and often, thinking he's escaping, runs straight into his opponent's arms.

At first, while still on the Kaluga road, Napoleon's armies made their presence known. But once they reached the Smolensk road, they ran with the bell's clapper held tight—and often, thinking they were escaping, ran right into the Russians.

Because of the speed of the French flight and the Russian pursuit, and the resulting exhaustion of the horses, the main means of determining the enemy's position—cavalry scouting—was unavailable. Besides, the frequent and rapid changes of position by both armies meant that even information received couldn't be delivered in time. If news came one day that the enemy had been at a certain position the day before, by the third day when anything could have been done, that army was already two days' march farther on and in a completely different spot.

One army fled and the other pursued. Beyond Smolensk there were several different roads available to the French, and one would have thought that during their four-day halt there they might have learned where the enemy was, devised a better plan, and tried something new. But after a four-day rest, the mob—with no strategy or plans—simply started running again along the beaten track, neither turning right nor left but taking the old, worst road through Krasnoe and Orsha.

Expecting the enemy from behind rather than ahead, the French spread out over a distance of twenty-four hours' march. At the very front fled the Emperor, then the kings, then the dukes. The Russian army, expecting Napoleon to take the road to the right beyond the Dnieper—which was the only sensible thing for him to do—turned right themselves and came out on the highway at Krasnoe. And here, as in a game of blindman's buff, the French ran into the Russian vanguard. Spotting their enemy unexpectedly, the French fell into confusion and froze with sudden fright, then resumed their flight, abandoning comrades who were farther behind. For three days, separate portions of the French army—first Murat's (the Viceroy's), then Davout's, then Ney's—ran the gauntlet of the Russian army. They abandoned one another, abandoned all their heavy baggage, artillery, and half their men, fleeing past the Russians at night by making wide detours to the right.

Ney, who came last, had been busy blowing up the walls of Smolensk, which were in nobody's way—because despite their desperate plight, or perhaps because of it, the French wanted to punish the floor they had stumbled on. Ney, who had started with a corps of ten thousand men, reached Napoleon at Orsha with only a thousand left, having abandoned all the rest along with his cannon, and having crossed the Dnieper by stealth at night at a wooded spot.

From Orsha they fled farther along the road to Vilna, still playing blindman's buff with the pursuing army. At the Berezina they fell into disarray again—many drowned, many surrendered—but those who got across the river fled on. Their supreme commander put on a fur coat and, climbing into a sleigh, galloped off alone, abandoning his companions. The others who could manage it drove away too, leaving those who could not to surrender or die.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: This campaign was essentially a flight during which the French did everything possible to destroy themselves. From the moment they turned onto the Kaluga road until the day their leader abandoned the army, not one movement of the mob made any sense. One might have expected that historians—who attribute the actions of the masses to the will of one man—would find it impossible to fit the story of this retreat into their framework. But no! Mountains of books have been written about this campaign, and everywhere we find descriptions of Napoleon's strategic arrangements, his maneuvers, and the deep plans that supposedly guided the army, as well as the military genius of his marshals.

The retreat from Malo-Yaroslavets, when Napoleon had a clear road into a well-supplied region and a parallel route that Kutuzov later followed—this needless retreat along a devastated road—is explained to us as the result of deep strategic thinking. Similarly profound reasoning is offered for his retreat from Smolensk to Orsha. Then his heroism at Krasnoe is described, where he supposedly stood ready to accept battle, took personal command, walked about with a birch stick, and said:
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general"—but then immediately ran away again, abandoning the scattered remnants of the army he left behind.
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general."

Then we are told of the greatness of soul of the marshals, especially of Ney—a greatness of soul that consisted in sneaking through the forest by night, crossing the Dnieper, and escaping to Orsha while abandoning his standards, artillery, and nine-tenths of his men.

And finally, the departure of the great Emperor from his heroic army is presented to us by historians as something noble and characteristic of genius. Even that final act of running away—which in plain language is the lowest depth of cowardice that every child is taught to be ashamed of—even that act finds justification in the historians' vocabulary.

When it becomes impossible to stretch the elastic threads of historical reasoning any further, when actions clearly violate everything humanity calls right or even just, historians produce their saving concept of "greatness." "Greatness," it seems, makes the standards of right and wrong irrelevant. For the "great" man, nothing is wrong; there is no crime for which a "great" man can be blamed.

"It is grand!" say the historians, and there is no longer any good or evil, only "grand" and "not grand." Grand is good, not grand is bad. Grand is the defining trait, in their view, of certain special creatures called "heroes." And Napoleon, escaping home in a warm fur coat while leaving his comrades—men he himself had brought there—to perish, feels that this is grand, and his conscience is at peace.
("It is grand.")
("That it is grand.")

"From the sublime (he saw something sublime in himself) to the ridiculous is but a step," he said. And the whole world has been repeating for fifty years: "Sublime! Grand! Napoleon the Great!" From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.
("From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.")
And it occurs to no one that to accept a kind of greatness that exists outside the standards of right and wrong is simply to admit one's own insignificance and boundless moral smallness.
For us, with the standard of good and evil given us by Christ, no human actions are beyond judgment. And there is no greatness where simplicity, goodness, and truth are absent.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: What Russian, reading the account of the final phase of the 1812 campaign, hasn't felt an uncomfortable sense of regret, dissatisfaction, and confusion? Who hasn't asked: how is it that the French weren't all captured or destroyed when three Russian armies had them surrounded with superior numbers, when the disorganized French were starving and freezing and surrendering in droves, and when—as historians tell us—the Russian aim was to stop the French, cut them off, and capture every last one of them?

How was it that the Russian army, which when outnumbered by the French had given battle at Borodino, failed to achieve its purpose when it had surrounded the French on three sides and its goal was to capture them? Can the French really be so enormously superior to us that when we had them surrounded with greater forces, we couldn't beat them? How could that happen?
History (or what passes for it) answers these questions by saying it happened because Kutuzov and Tormasov and Chichagov, and this man and that man, failed to carry out certain maneuvers...

But why didn't they carry out those maneuvers? And why, if they were at fault for not following a prearranged plan, weren't they tried and punished? But even if we admit that Kutuzov, Chichagov, and others were the cause of the Russian failures, it is still incomprehensible why, given the Russian army's positions at Krasnoe and the Berezina (where we had superior forces in both cases), Napoleon's army with its marshals, kings, and Emperor wasn't captured—if that was indeed what the Russians were aiming for.
The explanation offered by Russian military historians—that Kutuzov prevented an attack—is groundless, because we know he could not restrain his troops from attacking at Vyazma and Tarutino.

Why was the Russian army—which with inferior forces had held its own against the enemy at full strength at Borodino—defeated at Krasnoe and the Berezina by the disorganized crowds of the French, when it had numerical superiority?

If the aim of the Russians was to cut off and capture Napoleon and his marshals—and that aim was not merely frustrated but all attempts to achieve it were most shamefully foiled—then this last period of the campaign is quite rightly considered by the French to be a series of victories, and quite wrongly considered victorious by Russian historians.

Russian military historians, insofar as they submit to logic, must accept this conclusion, and despite all their lyrical praise of valor and devotion, must reluctantly admit that the French retreat from Moscow was a series of victories for Napoleon and defeats for Kutuzov.

But setting national pride entirely aside, one feels that such a conclusion involves a contradiction: the series of French "victories" brought the French complete destruction, while the series of Russian "defeats" led to the total annihilation of the enemy and the liberation of the country.

The source of this contradiction lies in the fact that historians, studying the letters of sovereigns and generals, memoirs, reports, and plans, have attributed to this final period of the 1812 war an aim that never existed—namely, the plan to cut off and capture Napoleon along with his marshals and army.
Such an aim never existed and could never have existed, because it would have been senseless and its achievement utterly impossible.

It would have been senseless, first, because Napoleon's disorganized army was already fleeing Russia at maximum speed—which was exactly what every Russian wanted. So what was the point of carrying out various operations against Frenchmen who were running away as fast as they possibly could?
Second, it would have been senseless to try to block the path of men whose every ounce of energy was directed at escape.

Third, it would have been senseless to sacrifice Russian troops in order to destroy a French army that, without any outside interference, was already destroying itself so rapidly that it couldn't carry across the border more than a hundredth part of its original strength—which is exactly what happened by December.

Fourth, it would have been senseless to want to capture the Emperor, kings, and dukes—whose capture would have been in the highest degree embarrassing for the Russians, as the most skillful diplomats of the time, including Joseph de Maistre and others, recognized. Even more senseless would have been the idea of capturing whole French army corps when the Russian army itself had shrunk by half before reaching Krasnoe, and a full division would have been needed just to guard the prisoners, while Russian soldiers weren't always getting full rations and the prisoners already taken were dying of hunger.

All the elaborate plans for cutting off and capturing Napoleon and his army were like the plan of a gardener who, when chasing a cow out of his garden after it trampled his flower beds, runs to the gate and hits the cow on the head. The only excuse for such a gardener would be that he was very angry. But not even that could be said for those who drew up this plan, since they weren't the ones whose flowers had been trampled.
But besides the fact that cutting off Napoleon and his army would have been senseless, it was also impossible.

It was impossible, first, because—as experience shows that a column's three-mile march on a battlefield never goes according to plan—the probability of Chichagov, Kutuzov, and Wittgenstein all arriving at the same place at the appointed time was so remote as to be effectively zero—as Kutuzov himself recognized when he received the plan and remarked that operations planned over great distances never produce the intended results.
Second, it was impossible because to halt the momentum with which Napoleon's army was retreating would have required forces incomparably greater than those the Russians possessed.

Third, it was impossible because the military term "to cut off" has no real meaning. You can cut off a slice of bread, but not an army. To cut off an army—to block its road—is quite impossible, because there is always plenty of room to get around, and there is the night when nothing can be seen, as the military theorists could have learned from the examples of Krasnoe and the Berezina. Prisoners can only be taken if they agree to be taken, just as you can only catch a swallow if it lands on your hand. Men can only be captured if they surrender according to the rules of strategy and tactics, as the Germans did. But the French saw no reason to comply, since death by starvation and cold awaited them equally whether they fled or surrendered.

Fourth and most importantly, it was impossible because never since the beginning of the world had a war been fought under such conditions as those of 1812, and the Russian army, in pursuing the French, had already strained itself to the breaking point and could not have done more without destroying itself.

During the movement of the Russian army from Tarutino to Krasnoe, it lost fifty thousand sick and stragglers—a number equal to the population of a large provincial city. Half the men fell out of the army without a single battle.

And it is about this period—when the army had no boots or sheepskin coats, was short of provisions and without vodka, camping in the snow at fifteen below zero for months on end, with only seven or eight hours of daylight, when men were taken into a realm of death where discipline breaks down, not just for a few hours as in battle but for months, where every moment they fought against hunger and cold, and half the army perished in a single month—it is about this period that historians tell us how Miloradovich should have flanked here and Tormasov should have marched there and Chichagov should have waded through knee-deep snow to somewhere else, and how so-and-so "routed" and "cut off" the French, and so on.

The Russians—half of whom died—did everything that could and should have been done to achieve a goal worthy of the nation. They are not to blame because other Russians, sitting in warm rooms, proposed that they should do the impossible.

All the strange contradiction between the facts and the historical accounts arises only because historians have written the history of the fine words and feelings of various generals, rather than the history of the events themselves.

To them, the speeches of Miloradovich seem fascinating, as do their own theories and the medals this or that general received. But the question of those fifty thousand men who were left in hospitals and graves doesn't even interest them, because it falls outside the scope of their investigation.

Yet one need only set aside the study of reports and staff plans and look at the movements of those hundreds of thousands of men who took a direct part in the events, and all the questions that seemed insoluble are resolved easily and simply.
The aim of cutting off Napoleon and his army never existed except in the imaginations of a dozen people. It could not exist because it was senseless and unachievable.

The people had one single aim: to free their land from invasion. That aim was achieved, first of all, on its own, as the French ran away, so it was only necessary not to stop their flight. Second, it was achieved by guerrilla warfare, which was destroying the French. And third, it was achieved by the fact that a large Russian army was following the French, ready to use force if their retreat should stop.
The Russian army had to act like a whip driving a running animal. And the experienced driver knew it was better to hold the whip raised as a threat than to strike the running animal on the head.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: When we see a dying animal, we feel a sense of horror: something made of the same substance as ourselves is perishing before our eyes. But when it is a beloved and intimate person who is dying, besides this horror at the extinguishing of life, there is a tearing apart, a spiritual wound that, like a physical wound, is sometimes fatal and sometimes heals, but always aches and flinches at any rough, irritating touch.

After Prince Andrew's death, Natasha and Princess Mary both felt this. Crushed in spirit and closing their eyes before the menacing cloud of death that hung over them, they dared not look life in the face. They carefully guarded their raw wounds from any harsh or painful contact. Everything—a carriage rattling quickly past in the street, a summons to dinner, the maid's question about what dress to prepare, or worst of all, any word of insincere or halfhearted sympathy—felt like an insult, painfully irritating the wound, interrupting the necessary silence in which they both tried to listen to the solemn and terrible chorus still echoing in their minds, and preventing them from gazing into those mysterious, infinite vistas that had for an instant opened before them.
Only when they were alone together were they free from such assaults. They spoke little even to each other, and when they did, it was about trivial things.

Both avoided any mention of the future. To acknowledge the possibility of a future seemed to them an insult to his memory. Even more carefully did they avoid anything connected with him who was dead. It seemed that what they had lived through and experienced could not be expressed in words, and that any reference to the details of his life would violate the majesty and sacredness of the mystery that had been accomplished before their eyes.

The constant restraint from speaking, the careful avoidance of everything that might lead to the forbidden subject—this halting on all sides at the boundary of what they could not mention—brought before their minds with even greater purity and clarity what they were both feeling.

But pure and complete grief is as impossible as pure and complete joy. Princess Mary, in her role as the sole and independent guardian of her own fate and of her nephew's upbringing, was the first to be called back to life from that realm of sorrow in which she had lived for the first two weeks. She received letters from relatives that required replies; the room where little Nicholas had been placed was damp and he began to cough; Alpatych came to Yaroslavl with reports on their affairs and suggestions that they return to Moscow, to the house on Vozdvizhenka Street, which had survived intact and needed only minor repairs. Life would not stand still, and it was necessary to go on living. Hard as it was for Princess Mary to emerge from her secluded world of contemplation, and sorry and almost ashamed as she felt to leave Natasha alone, the demands of daily life required her attention and she involuntarily yielded to them. She went through the accounts with Alpatych, consulted with Dessalles about her nephew, and gave orders and made preparations for the journey to Moscow.
Natasha was left alone and, from the time Princess Mary began preparing for departure, withdrew from her too.

Princess Mary asked the countess to let Natasha travel with her to Moscow, and both parents gladly accepted the offer, seeing their daughter losing strength every day and believing that a change of scene and Moscow doctors would do her good.
"I'm not going anywhere," Natasha replied when this was proposed. "Please just leave me alone!" And she ran out of the room, barely holding back tears of irritation and vexation rather than sorrow.

After feeling herself abandoned by Princess Mary and left alone in her grief, Natasha spent most of her time in her room by herself, sitting huddled up with her feet tucked under her in the corner of the sofa, tearing and twisting something with her slender, nervous fingers, staring intently at whatever her eyes happened to fall on. This solitude exhausted and tormented her, but she desperately needed it. The moment anyone came in, she would jump up quickly, change her position and expression, and pick up a book or some sewing, clearly waiting impatiently for the intruder to leave.
She felt as though at any moment she might break through to that thing on which—with a terrible questioning too great for her strength—her whole being was fixed.

One day toward the end of December, Natasha, pale and thin, dressed in a black woolen gown with her braided hair carelessly twisted into a knot, sat crouched with her feet tucked under her in the corner of the sofa, nervously crumpling and smoothing the end of her sash while staring at a corner of the door.

She was gazing in the direction he had gone—to the other side of life. And that other side of life, which she had never thought about before and which had always seemed so distant and improbable, was now nearer and more familiar and more real to her than this side, where everything was either emptiness and desolation or suffering and humiliation.
She was gazing toward where she knew him to be; but she could not picture him other than as he had been here. She saw him again as he had been at Mytishchi, at Troitsa, and at Yaroslavl.
She saw his face, heard his voice, repeated his words and her own, and sometimes invented other words they might have said.

There he is, lying back in an armchair in his velvet cloak, leaning his head on his thin, pale hand. His chest is terribly hollow and his shoulders raised. His lips are pressed firmly together, his eyes glitter, and a wrinkle comes and goes on his pale forehead. One of his legs twitches just perceptibly, but rapidly. Natasha knows he is struggling with terrible pain. "What is that pain like? Why does he have it? What does he feel? How does it hurt him?" she thought. He noticed her watching him, raised his eyes, and began to speak seriously:

"One thing would be terrible," he said, "to bind oneself forever to a suffering man. It would be continual torture." And he looked at her searchingly. Natasha, as usual, answered before she had time to think. She said: "This can't go on—it won't. You will get well—completely well."

She now replayed that scene from the beginning and relived what she had felt then. She recalled his long, sad, and severe look at those words and understood the meaning of the reproach and despair in that prolonged gaze.

"I agreed," Natasha now said to herself, "that it would be terrible if he always continued to suffer. I said it then only because it would have been terrible for him. But he understood it differently. He thought it would be terrible for me. He still wanted to live then, and he feared death. And I said it so clumsily and stupidly! I didn't say what I meant. I thought something entirely different. If I had said what I was actually thinking, I would have said: even if he had to go on dying, dying continually before my eyes, I would have been happy compared to what I am now. Now there is nothing... nobody. Did he know that? No. He didn't know and never will. And now it can never, never be put right." And now he seemed to be saying the same words to her again, but this time, in her imagination, Natasha gave him a different answer. She stopped him and said: "Terrible for you, but not for me! You know that there is nothing in life for me but you, and to suffer with you is the greatest happiness I could have." And he took her hand and pressed it as he had pressed it on that terrible evening four days before his death. And in her imagination she said other tender and loving words that she might have said then but only spoke now: "I love you!... You!... I love, love..." she whispered, clenching her hands together and gritting her teeth with desperate effort...

She was overcome by sweet sorrow and tears were already rising in her eyes; then suddenly she asked herself to whom she was saying this. Again everything was shrouded in hard, dry confusion, and again with a strained frown she peered toward the world where he was. And now—now it seemed she was about to penetrate the mystery... But at the instant when the incomprehensible seemed about to reveal itself, a loud rattle of the door handle struck painfully on her ears. Dunyasha, her maid, burst into the room quickly and abruptly, with a frightened look and no concern for her mistress.
"Come to your father at once, please!" she said with a strange, agitated look. "A misfortune... about Peter Ilyich... a letter," she finished with a sob.
